reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A collagenopathy usually caused by variants in COL2A1, COL11A1, or COL11A2, most types inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
The classic combination is ocular, orofacial, auditory, and articular features, reflecting the wide distribution of types II and XI collagen
High myopia that is congenital and non-progressive, with vitreous abnormalities, is characteristic and confers a high lifetime risk of retinal detachment
Orofacial features include midface hypoplasia, a flat nasal bridge, and the Pierre Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis, and cleft palate)
Sensorineural or mixed hearing loss is common and warrants formal audiological assessment
Early-onset osteoarthritis and mild spondyloepiphyseal changes contribute to joint pain and stiffness
Retinal detachment prophylaxis and prompt ophthalmology review are central because detachment can cause preventable blindness
Diagnosis integrates the multisystem clinical picture with dilated eye examination, audiometry, and molecular genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Stickler syndrome results from defects in the fibrillar collagens types II and XI, which are major structural components of the vitreous, cartilage, and inner ear. Variants in COL2A1 or the type XI collagen genes disrupt normal collagen fibril assembly, producing an abnormal vitreous gel that predisposes to retinal tears and detachment, cartilage that is prone to early degeneration and mild skeletal dysplasia, and inner-ear structures vulnerable to sensorineural hearing loss. The same collagen deficiency during craniofacial development underlies the midface and palatal anomalies, including the Pierre Robin sequence.
additionalDifferentials: Kniest dysplasia and other type II collagenopathies
Non-syndromic high myopia with retinal detachment
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus and vitreous examination by an ophthalmologist
Refraction to characterise congenital high myopia
Molecular genetic testing of COL2A1, COL11A1, and COL11A2
Skeletal survey or targeted imaging for spondyloepiphyseal changes
Cleft palate and airway assessment in infants with the Pierre Robin sequence
redFlags: New floaters, flashing lights, or a visual field shadow suggesting retinal detachment
Neonatal airway compromise from the Pierre Robin sequence
Acute painful red eye or trauma in a highly myopic patient
Feeding or respiratory difficulty in an infant with a cleft palate
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a normal lifespan, but vision is threatened by retinal detachment, which is the principal preventable cause of morbidity, and joint and hearing problems accumulate over time. Outcomes improve markedly with proactive ophthalmic surveillance and detachment prophylaxis.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in children presenting with isolated Pierre Robin sequence
Underestimating retinal detachment risk and failing to arrange ophthalmology surveillance
Overlooking hearing loss because ocular features dominate the picture
Assuming high myopia is simple refractive error rather than syndromic
Not offering genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Prophylactic retinal treatment (laser or cryotherapy retinopexy) and urgent surgical repair of retinal tears or detachment
Lifelong ophthalmic surveillance with refractive correction of high myopia and detachment safety-netting
Audiological assessment and hearing amplification for sensorineural or mixed loss
Manage early-onset osteoarthritis with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint protection
Cleft palate repair and airway management for Pierre Robin sequence in infancy
Genetic counselling and family cascade screening for the autosomal dominant collagen variants
Multidisciplinary coordination across ophthalmology, audiology, orthopaedics and clinical genetics
